article.title: The most useful part of our release notes is the list of things we refuse to do for you
article.description: Threadplane 0.1.0 is out — an MIT Angular framework for agent UIs on LangGraph and AG-UI. The section worth reading first is the one that says where the library stops.

draft.text:
Threadplane 0.1.0 shipped this week. It is an Angular framework for building agent UIs on LangGraph and AG-UI, it is MIT, and every capability is in the free tier because there is no other tier.

I want to write about one section of the release notes instead of the whole list, because it is the section I would read first if someone handed me this library.

## The list that says where it stops

Here is what Threadplane does **not** do for you, and will not quietly start doing in a patch release:

- **The agent endpoint sits behind your proxy.** The browser should not talk to your graph server directly.
- **API keys never reach the bundle.** There is no config option that makes this safe, so there is no config option.
- **Thread IDs are server-generated.** Never mint one client-side.
- **CORS is yours to configure.**
- **The interrupt panel is yours to compose.** `<chat>` does not render it. The primitives ship; the review experience is a product decision.
- **The resume payload is yours to choose.** Only you know what "approved" means in your domain.
- **Tracing and evaluation are yours.** Runs get traced by tools built for tracing, not by a UI library.

A feature list is a sales document unless it also says where it stops. Every row above is a place where taking the work off your hands would mean taking a decision off your hands too — and the ones I would most regret automating are the security ones.

## What it does do

The pitch is narrow on purpose: the last mile. Everything between "my agent streams tokens" and "my team can put this in front of a customer."

- `<chat>` plus 15 documented components — message list, input, tool-call cards, reasoning, trace, subagent cards, sidebar, popup, debug
- Streaming markdown over a 26-node registry, sanitized, with per-instance overrides
- Durable threads: persistence, checkpoints, durable execution, time travel
- Interrupts and human approvals
- Client tools that run in the browser and hand control back to the graph
- Generative UI via json-render and A2UI v0.9, rendering only components you registered
- Subagents as their own cards with their own transcripts
- The five Deep Agents capabilities — planning, filesystem, subagents, memory, skills
- `AgentError` classifying every failure as `connection`, `auth`, `server`, `interrupted`, or `aborted`, each with a `retryable` flag
- A test path that runs with no model and no API key

## The runtime is not a one-way door

`@threadplane/langgraph` and `@threadplane/ag-ui` both produce the same `Agent` interface — six signals, four methods, one event stream. Components written against `<chat>` do not know which backend they are talking to. When the backend changes, your providers change and your components do not.

I measured that rather than asserting it. Across three capability demos built twice, the same six of nine files differ every time, and four of those six are not application code.

The AG-UI side is protocol-first, so it got tested against runtimes that have nothing to do with LangGraph: AWS Strands, Microsoft Agent Framework, and Mastra. Three runtimes, two languages, no adapter changes for messages, tool calls, or state. Each has a standalone example and a committed transcript of its wire traffic.

## About the version number

Through `v0.0.66` this project bumped only the patch digit. Fifty-five commits of accumulated breaking changes shipped under a counter that said nothing had broken.

That is not semver, and by the end the published packages were contradicting the documentation. So 0.1.0 is not a feature release. It is the release where the version number starts telling the truth. Six packages move as one fixed group, because an adapter and the surface it feeds are not independently upgradable in practice.

## The free part

There is no open-core split. No capability is held back, no seat count, no activation, no runtime license check, no account.

There are paid offerings and I want to be precise about what they sell: review time, a private channel, and a response commitment. They sell my attention. They do not sell code you cannot otherwise have.

The moment a capability moves behind a paywall, every architectural decision in the library starts getting made by the pricing page, and you can feel that in the code long before you see it on the invoice.

Try it without a backend first — it runs a fake agent in the browser, so you can see the UI before you stand up a server:

```bash
npm install @threadplane/chat @threadplane/langgraph @langchain/core @langchain/langgraph-sdk marked
```

Full write-up with the complete capability table: https://threadplane.ai/blog/threadplane-0-1-0

If you try it, I would rather hear where it broke than that it was nice.
